title: Who Has Buried the Dead?: From Stalin to Putin … The last great secret of World War Two
author: Raymond H. Thompson
target_audience: Historians and scholars interested in World War II and Soviet history
General readers seeking insight into 20th-century history and its contemporary ramifications
Individuals interested in the intersection of politics and memory
core_themes: Soviet and Russian manipulation of historical memory
Enduring legacies of WWII in post-Soviet Russia
primary_purpose: To investigate the persistent secrecy, obfuscation, and manipulation surrounding the Katyn massacre and related atrocities from the era of Stalinist terror through Putin’s Russia, and to analyze how these unresolved historical crimes have shaped politics, identity, and historical memory in Russia and beyond.

structure_format.organization: Chronological with thematic exploration of political, social, and cultural impacts, supported by archival research and eyewitness accounts
features: Contextual analysis linking past to present
Discussion of ongoing relevance in current Russian politics

key_concepts_lessons: The Katyn massacre was one of the most significant and contested atrocities of WWII, emblematic of broader patterns of state violence and denial.
Control over historical narrative is a potent political tool, employed by both Stalinist and modern Russian authorities.
Truth about state crimes remains at risk in authoritarian and semi-authoritarian regimes, with memory manipulated for political ends.
Historical amnesia and selective remembrance affect international relations and domestic policy in Russia and other post-Soviet states.
Reckoning with past atrocities is essential for justice, reconciliation, and the prevention of future abuses.
style_tone: Engaged with moral and historical questions
notable_features: Blends historical scholarship with journalistic investigation
Uncovers new evidence and perspectives on the Katyn massacre
Links historical events to contemporary Russian politics under Putin
Examines the international implications of unresolved historical crimes
cultural_historical_context: The book was published during renewed Russian efforts to control historical memory, particularly concerning WWII, and at a time when the legacies of Stalinism and the unresolved traumas of the 20th century remain central in Russian statecraft, propaganda, and foreign policy.
reception_impact: Well-received among historians and scholars of Eastern Europe
Praised for its rigorous research and accessibility for a general audience
Noted for its timely exploration of the intersections of history, truth, and power
Contributes to public debate on historical denial and the politics of memory

Bloodlands: Europe Between Hitler and Stalin by Timothy Snyder
